newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Airbus crash case goes to court.
newsitem.headline: French Airbus crash case goes to court.

text.p: Two Air France airline executives and two pilots flying an Airbus airliner when it crashed at an airshow in 1988 went on trial on manslaughter charges on Friday.

Three people died and some 50 were injured when the plane, which had been flying only a few dozen metres (yards) above the ground on a demonstration flight, hit treetops and crashed in a forest in eastern France.

The pilots Michel Asseline and Pierre Mazieres, since sacked by Air France, air operations chief Henri Petit and security manager Jacques Gauthier will all stand trial for alleged manslaughter and involuntarily causing injuries.
Petit is accused of breaking a ban on such flights carrying passengers and authorising the plane to fly too low.

Francois Furstengerger, president of the aeroclub in the Alsatian town of Habsheim where the Airbus Industrie A320 passenger plane crashed with 130 people on board, will face the same charges, they said.
Asseline and Mazieres blamed the engines, the computer system, and the controls for the crash.
They accused French authorities of interfering with the plane's black box to hide its faults at a time when the plane was being launched on the market place.
An investigating magistrate said studies had shown such interference was "impossible and absurd".
The magistrate blamed human error. Experts say the pilots flew too slowly and too low, and regained altitude too late.
Survivors of the crash said they doubted the trial, which is expected to last a month, would shed light on the accident.
"We'll be at the trial because the association (of victims) is a civil plaintiff, but we don't have any illusions," said Jean-Marie Schreiber, the association's president.
Airbus is a consortium made up of France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc, Construcciones Aeronauticas SA of Spain and the Daimler-Benz Aerospace unit of Germany's Daimler-Benz AG.
